segments.text: The new United States had to prove republican government could actually survive and function — this topic follows that experiment from a weak confederation through a strengthened federal Constitution to the establishment of durable institutions and parties.

items.text: The first ten constitutional amendments, central to securing broader acceptance of the new federal Constitution.
Prepare the Constitution separately, then make president cards for Washington, Adams, Jefferson, Madison and Monroe: one domestic development, one foreign-policy issue, one lasting significance each.
Do not say the Constitution immediately solved all problems; party conflict, slavery and federal-state disputes continued.
Do not confuse the Articles of Confederation with the later federal Constitution.
Do not portray the War of 1812 as a simple U.S. military victory; outcomes were mixed.
The Constitutional Convention met in 1787; the new Constitution entered into operation in 1789; the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791.
The Louisiana Purchase (1803) roughly doubled U.S. territory.
The War of 1812 ended with the Treaty of Ghent (1814), restoring the prewar territorial situation.
Treat the early republic as an experiment in making the Constitution actually work while the country simultaneously expanded and faced European pressure.
Party competition emerged in practice despite the founders’ explicit design intent against factions — a useful example of institutions evolving beyond their founders’ original expectations.
